title: Blood
note: Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma, about 92% water, carries the formed elements. Erythrocytes carry oxygen on hemoglobin, leukocytes defend the body, and platelets start clotting. Hemostasis runs in three steps: vascular spasm, platelet plug, and coagulation, which ends with thrombin turning fibrinogen into fibrin.

read.title: Stopping a leak
text: When a vessel is cut, the body does not rely on a single mechanism. Hemostasis runs in three overlapping steps. First comes vascular spasm: smooth muscle in the vessel wall contracts and narrows the opening, cutting blood loss within seconds.

Second, platelets form a plug. Normally they slide past the smooth endothelium, but at a wound they meet exposed collagen. With help from von Willebrand factor they stick, change shape, and release chemicals such as ADP and serotonin that recruit more platelets and keep the vessel constricted.

Third, coagulation turns the loose plug into a firm clot. Damaged tissue releases tissue factor, which starts the fast extrinsic pathway, while contact activation of factor XII starts the slower intrinsic pathway within the blood itself. Both pathways converge on factor X and lead to the enzyme thrombin. Thrombin cuts soluble fibrinogen into fibrin strands that mesh over the plug and trap red cells. Calcium is needed at many steps, and the liver needs vitamin K to make several of the factors.
A clot is meant to be temporary. As the vessel heals, plasmin, activated from plasminogen, digests the fibrin, while anticoagulants such as antithrombin keep clotting from spreading beyond the wound.
